Gardaí believe man missing for over five weeks was stabbed and his body hidden by his attacker LAST UPDATE | 29 Jul GARDAÍ BELIEVE A man who disappeared five weeks ago in Dublin was stabbed to death in an apartment in Dublin and his body concealed by his attacker. The victim, Charlie ‘Lachy’ Clarke (67), was last seen in June by his family. After five weeks they went to gardaí at the weekend to report him missing. It is believed that Clarke, who was known to gardaí and originally from Limerick, was attacked in his home, an apartment at Viking Harbour, near Victoria Quay in Dublin 8. The garda theory is that his body was then taken from there and disposed of by his attacker or people linked to the suspect. It is understood his family did not formally report him missing to gardaí and instead put up posters around the area in Dublin looking for him. Advertisement They checked if he was in garda stations and hospitals and posted online looking for help to find him. As they became increasingly concerned they then went to a garda station last Sunday and reported him missing. Gardaí immediately began an investigation. Rapidly gardaí determined that it was a criminal matter, and they believe he was likely stabbed to death. https://www.politico.eu/article/mep-mano.text: PARIS — Manon Aubry, co-chair of the Left Group in the European Parliament, was back on her feet Thursday after being hospitalized for a snake bite. “I was in the (French region of) Lot and I simply stepped on a viper,” Aubry told reporters on the first day of a conference in southern France by her hard-left party, France Unbowed. Aubry on Tuesday shared a picture of herself on a hospital bed after the incident, drawing widespread media attention in France. Advertisement Advertisement “I’d made that Instagram post precisely to avoid questions … I hadn’t anticipated a newswire dispatch on the subject,” she said. Aubry said Thursday that she was “unlucky,” as France typically only sees about 150 similar venomous snake bites and two serious cases a year. “At the hospital where I was treated, they told me they hadn’t seen one in 10 years,” she said. The 36-year-old then struck a more positive tone, calling the meeting an important moment for her party’s leader and presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who has gained momentum since announcing his candidacy in May. “I see a tiny opening here — we’re going to win in 2027.”

http://www.bgnes.com/european-union/hybr.text: The European Union and its member states are facing an escalating hybrid campaign that over the past two years has included cyberattacks, information operations, interference in elections, sabotage, attacks on critical infrastructure, physical assaults, airspace violations and the use of unmanned aerial vehicles. In its official documents, the EU defines hybrid threats as coordinated actions that may combine information manipulation, cyberattacks, economic pressure, covert political activity, sabotage and other tools designed to weaken or destabilise a state or institution. The European Union has officially stated that Russia is conducting large-scale and coordinated hybrid campaigns against the EU and its member states aimed at undermining Europe’s security, resilience and democratic foundations, while weakening European support for Ukraine. Not every incident examined, however, has been conclusively attributed to the Russian state. Germany and Czechia targeted by Russian cyber-espionage operationOne of the clearest documented cases involves cyberattacks attributed to Russia’s GRU military intelligence agency and the APT28 group linked to it. Germany announced in May 2024 that APT28 had carried out cyberattacks against German political organisations, including email accounts belonging to the leadership of the Social Democratic Party, as well as government bodies and organisations in the logistics, defence, aerospace and technology sectors. The attacks exploited what was then an unknown critical vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook and compromised multiple email accounts. The German government formally attributed the operation to Russia and its military intelligence service, and Berlin summoned a Russian diplomatic representative over the attacks. Czechia also reported attacks against its institutions by the same Russian cyber actor. NATO backed the German and Czech attribution of the attacks to APT28 and the GRU and said similar activity had affected other allies. The case demonstrated that cyberattacks are increasingly viewed not simply as criminal activity, but as part of state-organised hybrid campaigns against political and strategic targets in Europe. Romania: A hybrid attack on the electoral processOne of the most serious cases of the past two years involved Romania’s presidential election in November and December 2024. Romanian authorities identified large-scale cyberattacks against election-related systems alongside coordinated activity on social media. According to declassified Romanian intelligence documents, more than 85,000 cyberattacks were detected between November 20 and 26, 2024. The attacks continued on election day and through the following night. At the same time, authorities identified coordinated activity on social media, including the use of numerous accounts and mechanisms designed to artificially boost the visibility of content supporting independent candidate Călin Georgescu. Romanian intelligence agencies described the country as a target of aggressive Russian hybrid activity. Romania and the EU later characterised the events as a complex Russian hybrid attack that had a significant impact on the electoral process. Romania’s Constitutional Court annulled the entire presidential election process after receiving declassified information concerning irregularities, manipulation on social media and problems with campaign transparency. The case is particularly significant because it illustrates a different model of hybrid attack, one in which the main objective is not the physical destruction of infrastructure but the reshaping of the political environment, the erosion of trust in elections and the deepening of an institutional crisis. Incendiary parcels turned European logistics networks into a targetA series of attacks involving self-igniting parcels sent through European logistics and postal networks began in July 2024. Four parcels were sent from Lithuania to addresses in Britain and Poland. One caught fire at Leipzig/Halle Airport before it could be loaded onto an aircraft. Other parcels ignited at a warehouse in Britain and inside a truck in Poland, while a fourth was intercepted intact. The investigation subsequently developed into an international operation involving German, Lithuanian, Dutch, Polish and British authorities, coordinated by Eurojust and supported by Europol. In March 2026, Eurojust said the investigation had identified 22 suspects in Lithuania and Poland who were believed to have acted on behalf of Russian military intelligence. The case revealed a model in which intermediaries were recruited through messaging applications, assigned separate tasks and paid in cryptocurrency. The investigation remains ongoing, and the suspicions do not amount to final court convictions. Poland uncovered preparations for further sabotageIn October 2025, Polish prosecutors opened an investigation into individuals suspected of acting in the interests of Russian intelligence services and preparing further acts of sabotage. According to prosecutors, the plans involved parcels containing explosive and incendiary materials intended for shipment to Ukraine and designed to ignite or explode during transportation. The investigation concerns alleged activity by a foreign intelligence service against Poland and allied countries. Polish authorities said the planned operations were intended to spread fear among the population and destabilise European countries supporting Ukraine. Polish railway sabotage highlighted pressure on critical infrastructureIn November 2025, Poland was hit by two serious acts of sabotage targeting railway line No. 7 between Warsaw East and Dorohusk, on the route towards Lublin and the Ukrainian border. On November 15, a C4 explosive device was placed on the railway near Mika and detonated beneath a passing freight train. Near Gołąb, the overhead electrical network was damaged and specially designed metal objects were placed on the track, potentially capable of derailing a train. Polish prosecutors described the incidents as acts of sabotage of a terrorist nature carried out for the benefit of a foreign intelligence service. On November 19, prosecutors said the evidence pointed with a high degree of probability to two Ukrainian nationals as the direct perpetrators, allegedly acting on behalf of Russian intelligence. This remains the position of investigators rather than a final court judgment. Prime Minister Donald Tusk told the Polish parliament that the two men had cooperated with Russian services and described the case as possibly the most serious threat to Poland’s national security since the beginning of the Russia-Ukraine war. The Polish government introduced the third-level CHARLIE security alert for certain railway lines and launched Operation Horizon, which envisaged deploying up to 10,000 military personnel to protect critical infrastructure. Polish authorities also reported a subsequent disinformation campaign aimed at shifting responsibility for the sabotage onto Ukraine and discrediting Poland’s security services. Baltic Sea undersea cables become a new frontOn December 25, 2024, the Estlink 2 electricity cable connecting Finland and Estonia was damaged. Finnish authorities took control of the Cook Islands-flagged tanker Eagle S and began investigating its possible connection to the damage. Finland’s National Bureau of Investigation opened a criminal investigation into aggravated property damage and interference with communications, while customs authorities launched a separate inquiry related to sanctions and the vessel’s cargo. The police preliminary investigation concluded in June 2025 and found a strong link between the Eagle S dragging its anchor and the damage to the cable. Senior crew members were charged. A court initially declined to hear the charges because of a jurisdictional issue, and prosecutors appealed. As of August 12, 2026, there is no final conviction establishing intent, nor has a Russian state order behind the incident been publicly proven. The case is particularly sensitive because it forms part of a wider series of incidents involving undersea communications and energy cables in the Baltic Sea. The documented damage and the established link to a specific vessel do not in themselves prove that the incident was a Russian state operation. NATO responds with Baltic SentryFollowing the series of incidents involving undersea infrastructure, NATO launched Baltic Sentry in January 2025. The Alliance increased its military presence in the Baltic Sea, deploying frigates, maritime patrol aircraft, national surveillance assets and new technologies, including a small fleet of naval drones. The aim is to improve surveillance of critical undersea infrastructure, detect suspicious activity more quickly and enable a faster response to future sabotage attempts. NATO has also strengthened coordination with private-sector companies that own and operate critical undersea infrastructure. Russia increases pressure on European airspaceViolations of NATO members’ airspace reached a new level in September 2025. During the night of September 9-10, numerous drones originating from Russia entered Polish airspace. NATO described the incident as a serious violation and responded with air defence and surveillance assets. The Alliance’s initial assessment did not publicly determine whether the incursion had been deliberate. Poland requested consultations under Article 4 of the North Atlantic Treaty. On September 12, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte announced Eastern Sentry, designed to strengthen the Alliance’s defensive posture across its entire eastern flank. The mission includes fighter jets, air-defence systems, reconnaissance aircraft and other assets, with particular emphasis on technologies designed to counter drones. France subsequently deployed three Rafale fighter jets to Poland, while NATO also began AWACS surveillance flights over the eastern flank. Estonia and other allies also report airspace violationsFollowing the incident in Poland, NATO said other allies, including Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway and Romania, had also recently been affected by Russian violations of their airspace. On September 19, 2025, three armed Russian MiG-31 fighter jets violated Estonian airspace for more than ten minutes. Estonia also requested consultations under Article 4. The North Atlantic Council said Russia bore full responsibility for the series of violations and warned that such actions created a risk of escalation and miscalculation. NATO said it would use all necessary military and non-military tools to defend its allies and reaffirmed its commitment to Article 5. Drones emerge as a separate dimension of the hybrid threatThe growing number of drone-related incidents accelerated efforts to build a common European approach on top of existing national measures and earlier EU strategies. On February 11, 2026, the European Commission presented an Action Plan on Drone and Counter-Drone Security. The plan calls for better prevention, improved drone detection, stronger coordination of responses and greater European defence preparedness. It also envisages the deployment of counter-drone systems to protect critical infrastructure and the EU’s external borders. Funding of €250 million has been announced for surveillance of land and maritime borders. The European Commission also plans to examine a common European regulatory framework for counter-drone systems, the possible creation of rapid-response teams for drone threats and large-scale annual European exercises. In the defence sector, the EU plans to accelerate the development of affordable and effective drone and counter-drone technologies. The EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance envisaged in the plan was formally launched on July 17, 2026. Germany builds its own counter-drone capabilityGermany has also developed dedicated institutional capacity to counter drone threats. The Federal Police established a specialised counter-drone unit, while federal and regional authorities opened a joint coordination centre on December 17, 2025. The measures were introduced amid a rise in unauthorised drone flights near critical infrastructure and airports, and suspicions that foreign state actors may be behind some of them. In August 2026, Leipzig/Halle Airport again became the focus of the German security services. During the night of August 4-5, a drone equipped with an explosive device and detonator was discovered at the airport. German authorities described the incident as a serious threat, and the federal prosecutor’s office took over the investigation on August 6. The case is particularly sensitive because of the airport’s strategic importance as a major European logistics hub and its role in transport operations linked, among other things, to Ukraine and NATO. As of August 12, 2026, however, German authorities have not publicly and conclusively attributed this specific incident to Russia. The incident itself is documented, but any assessment of Russian state responsibility must remain separate from an investigation that has not yet been completed. EU creates dedicated sanctions regime against hybrid activitiesThe European Union has not limited its response to political condemnation. On October 8, 2024, the Council of the EU established a dedicated sanctions framework targeting individuals and entities responsible for Russia’s destabilising activities. The framework covers sabotage, cyberattacks, attacks against critical infrastructure, information manipulation and interference, election interference and other hybrid activities. On December 16, 2024, the EU imposed its first sanctions under the new mechanism, targeting 16 individuals and three entities. Among them was Unit 29155 of Russia’s GRU military intelligence service, which the EU has linked to destabilising operations, assassinations, bomb attacks and cyber operations in Europe. Individuals associated with Russia’s Doppelganger information campaign were also included. Sanctions expanded in 2025 and 2026Throughout 2025 and 2026, the EU continued to expand sanctions against individuals and organisations linked to Russian hybrid campaigns. In December 2025, the Council sanctioned another 12 individuals and two entities over information manipulation and malicious cyber activity. In January 2026, another six individuals were sanctioned for foreign information manipulation and interference. Four more individuals were added in March 2026, while two additional entities were sanctioned in April over their involvement in Russia’s information infrastructure and propaganda activities. The European response is therefore targeting an expanding range of individuals, organisations and networks that the EU links to Russian hybrid campaigns across the physical, cyber and information domains. EU strengthens protection of undersea infrastructureFollowing the series of incidents in the Baltic Sea, the European Commission and the EU High Representative developed a common European approach to protecting undersea cables. The measures include tougher security requirements, risk assessments, better surveillance, faster detection of damage, quicker repairs, greater redundancy in communications networks and the development of more resilient cable systems. The EU is also increasing coordination with NATO, which is implementing Baltic Sentry. National measures to protect undersea infrastructure are thus increasingly being reinforced by broader European and Euro-Atlantic coordination. NATO expands permanent surveillanceNATO’s response to hybrid threats has also evolved substantially. The Alliance uses a range of mechanisms to counter hybrid threats, including Counter-Hybrid Support Teams, which can be deployed to member states at their request. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqly.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images By Nardine Saad Published 5 hours ago US President Donald Trump has announced that he will form an "AI Force" and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar amid warnings about the emergent technology. In a social media post on Saturday, he said his administration "will not in any way hinder or stifle the growth" of the industry, and pushed back against calls to slow down the development of AI until better safeguards are put in place. His post came as a slew of warnings about the potential dangers of AI have spurred calls for coordinated action on the technology's development. Trump offered no details or a timeline for his plan. Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings Published 3 days ago "AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country's GDP," he said on social media, adding that he wants the US to continue leading China in AI. AI now sits at the heart of the US-China rivalry as the world's two largest economies seek to gain an edge in advanced tech, and it is expected to be discussed when Trump meets President Xi Jinping next week. Meanwhile, Trump said his administration would use the existing criminal and civil justice system to target any bad actors using the AI. He also repeated comments that criticism and concerns around the potential dangers of AI are a "hoax". Figure caption, Watch: Cyber Correspondent Joe Tidy considers if could AI wipe out humanity, and how it might do it Claims by current and former researchers that the tech will endanger humanity - with one suggesting there is a greater than 10% chance of it "killing all humans" - have raised alarm bells in recent weeks. Major AI companies have been racing to develop better systems, including creating what they call super intelligence - theoretical tech which is smarter than humans. AI titans Anthropic, OpenAI and Google - the tech companies behind Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini, respectively - have also disclosed instances of security breaches or incidents in which their chatbots were used for "malicious activity". Anthropic head Dario Amodei recently called for AI development to slow down and proposed industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development. Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of xAI have both said they agree with his recommendations. Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic, told BBC that a "kill switch" that can be checked by a third party may need to be mandatory for the industry. The warnings have prompted US lawmakers to propose legislation around the technology but Altman suggested this week that Washington has struggled to keep pace with the new tech and how to regulate it. He said people should have more faith in AI firms to keep it safe. "The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Altman told a conference in San Francisco. In the UK, MPs across parties and peers have identified human rights risks posed by artificial intelligence and have argued that existing laws are ill-equipped to address the technology's rapid growth. The Joint Committee on Human Rights (JCHR) has published a report calling for a new bill on AI to "address the scale and seriousness" of such threats. https://www.baltictimes.com/foreign_mini.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Foreign Ministry has not received information from security agencies warranting closure of visa centers in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan 2026-09-28 LETA/TBT Staff RIGA - The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has not received any information from Latvian security agencies warranting the closure of visa centers in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, the ministry's press secretary Liga Jermacane told LETA. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it would make an appropriate decision if such information was received. The ministry's press secretary indicated that Latvia, based on an agreement concluded in 2015 with the outsourcing provider VF Worldwide Holdings, uses the outsourcing provider's services to accept visa applications in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. Visa applications are accepted at these visa centers and forwarded for review to the Latvian embassies in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. As reported, Lithuania is closing its visa centers in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Bosnia and Herzegovina for security reasons. These centers, whose operations were managed by an outsourcing provider, accepted applications for visas and residence permits. Lithuanian Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas emphasized that these offices act as intermediaries between foreign nationals and Lithuanian authorities - they accept applications for residence permits and initiate migration procedures. He explained that, after assessing security risks and terrorist threats, Katelynas sees no reason why such services should remain in these countries. The minister noted that this decision was made in light of warnings from the Lithuanian State Security Department regarding potential terrorist risks. "When the State Security Department warns of potential terrorism risks and has already identified individuals from Central Asia with radical views or links to terrorism, the state cannot wait for a risk to become an incident," the minister said.
